a2816.speech: Had said she opposed Trump's request to cut the PEPFAR funding ; after the lunch meeting with Vought, she said she still wanted detailed information about the proposals.

a2816.speaker: Democrats
a2816.speech: Warn a partisan cut now could make it more difficult to negotiate government funding bills that must pass by September 30 to avoid a shutdown.

a2832.speaker: Malawi Economic Justice Network (Mejn)
a2832.speech: has warned that a proposed United States bill to impose a five percent tax on all remittances sent abroad could significantly reduce the volume of funds flowing into Malawi from the diaspora, with far-reaching consequences for the country's already strained foreign exchange position.

a2832.speaker: Bertha Phiri, Mejn executive director
a2832.speech: said the tax, if passed into law, would add to the economic pressures Malawi is currently facing, particularly in light of recent aid cuts: "We are already in an environment where donors are cutting funding to Malawi," citing the United States Agency for International Development's (USAid) scaling down of financial support ; "If this persists, then we can expect that the forex problems might worsen. This could also affect our ability to import fuel and fertiliser. The impact on the economy would be huge."

a2832.speaker: Bertha Phiri, Mejn executive director
a2832.speech: further warned that taxing formal remittance channels could drive senders toward informal networks, reducing transparency and weakening the capacity of regulators to track inflows and design effective policy responses.

a2832.speaker: TheGlobalEconomy.com (data)
a2832.speech: According to its data, Malawi received approximately $260.4 million in personal remittances in 2023, down slightly from $264.3 million in 2022, representing about 1.85 percent of the country's Gross Domestic Product.

a2832.speaker: United Kingdom-based Malawian (anonymous)
a2832.speech: said it has now become a norm to send remittances back home using individuals, rather than authorised dealer banks (ADBs): "We just have to find people who can give me kwacha back home and I either give them pounds here or I make purchases on their behalf at an agreed rate. This is much better because now with the official rate at K2 224 against the pound, the rate can go up to K4 000 depending on how we negotiate."

a2835.speaker: Dr Ousmane Bougouma, President of Burkina Faso's Transitional Legislative Assembly (ALT)
a2835.speech: called on the international community to show as much interest in the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) as in the Palestinian and Lebanese crises: "The situation in Palestine and Lebanon recalls that of Burkina Faso, or of the countries of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) which are prey to acts of terrorism" ; "Our wish is that the international mobilisation for Palestine and Lebanon can also be observed in favour of the Sahelian cause, so that peace returns."

a2835.speaker: Extraordinary Arab-Islamic Summit (declaration)
a2835.speech: expressed the need to support peace efforts, resulting in a declaration for the liberation of its occupied territories, an immediate ceasefire, the lifting of the blockade on Gaza to allow the entry of humanitarian aid convoys and the holding of an international peace conference.

a3193.speaker: UN Independent Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory (report)
a3193.speech: Published a damning report concluding that a “genocide” has been committed in Gaza, finding that Israel committed four of the five acts constituting the crime of genocide as defined by the 1948 Convention ; The report directly accuses the most senior Israeli officials, including President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant, of not only having tolerated but also incited the commission of such crimes.

a3193.speaker: Volker Türk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a3193.speech: Denounced before the Human Rights Council the Israeli strike of 9 September in Doha targeting Hamas negotiators, stating that the attack in Qatar “constitutes a flagrant violation of international law, an attack on regional peace and a blow to the integrity of mediation processes worldwide” ; According to him, striking a delegation engaged in ceasefire talks amounts to undermining Qatar's role as mediator and compromising international diplomatic efforts.

a3193.speaker: Volker Türk, UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a3193.speech: Stressed in his address that the Israeli strike in Doha coincided with other actions “definitively undermining” any prospect of a two-State solution ; “War without rules is a future of endless cruelty,” warned the High Commissioner, calling on member States to act: to halt arms deliveries, exert maximum pressure for a ceasefire, demand the release of hostages and arbitrary detainees, and guarantee the delivery of humanitarian aid.

a3193.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General, and the members of the Security Council
a3193.speech: Also condemned this operation, judged contrary to the right to life and to the fundamental principles of humanitarian law.

a3193.speaker: Navi Pillay, President of the UN Commission of Inquiry and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a3193.speech: “It is clear that there is an intent to destroy, in whole or in part, the Palestinian population of Gaza.”

a3193.speaker: Navi Pillay, President of the UN Commission of Inquiry and former UN High Commissioner for Human Rights
a3193.speech: Recalled that “every day without action costs lives and undermines the credibility of international institutions.”

a3193.speaker: Francesca Albanese, UN Special Rapporteur on the Palestinian territories
a3193.speech: For her part denounced an offensive aimed at “making the city of Gaza uninhabitable” as part of a “broader plan of ethnic cleansing” ; According to her, Israel is using “unconventional weapons” to force the city's 800,000 refugees to flee ; “This is not a future risk, it is already under way: entire neighbourhoods are being wiped off the map,” she declared before the accredited correspondents in Geneva, Switzerland.

a3193.speaker: Francesca Albanese, UN Special Rapporteur on the Palestinian territories
a3193.speech: For Francesca Albanese, the “ongoing genocide” is not only Israel's responsibility but “that of the whole world,” which makes itself complicit through its inaction and through the continued sale of arms.

a3194.speaker: World Food Programme (WFP) (statement)
a3194.speech: Warned on Tuesday that 3.6 million people in Ethiopia overall are at risk of losing access to food aid in the coming weeks unless new financial support can urgently be sourced ; “WFP is being forced to halt treatment for 650 000 malnourished women and children in May due to insufficient funding” ; Said it had planned to reach two million mothers and children with life-saving nutrition assistance in 2025 but will fall short due to a predicted funding shortfall of US$222m between April and September ; “Cash and in-kind food assistance for up to one million refugees will stop in June if additional funding is not received.”

a3303.speaker: Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger (the three AES states)
a3303.speech: Have asserted that their departure from the grouping was "irreversible" ; accuse Ecowas leaders of being puppets of France, the former colonial power in the region.

a3303.speaker: Alliance of Sahel States (AES)
a3303.speech: Has stated that the free movement of people and goods from Ecowas countries would still be permitted in the three countries despite this departure.

a3303.speaker: Omar Alieu Touray, Gambian head of the Ecowas secretariat
a3303.speech: Summed it up in his address to a meeting of the council of foreign affairs ministers in Abuja last week: "Recent deliberations have underlined the importance of mediation and dialogue in resolving urgent problems. As we move forward, let us collectively renew our commitment to sustainable development, integration and the well-being of our citizens."

a3536.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of International Relations and Trade
a3536.speech: Says the ministry’s restructuring reflects the government’s strategic vision to enhance economic diplomacy and expand Namibia’s footprint in the continental and global economy; addressing ministry staff, emphasized the developmental priorities outlined in the Swapo Party Manifesto and its implementation plan, and stressed that economic diplomacy has always been a core function and pillar of Namibia’s policy on international relations and cooperation.

a3536.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of International Relations and Trade
a3536.speech: Implored those who have served in the ministry to embrace the transition with openness, recognizing the value and depth that the trade function and staff bring to the merged ministry: “Likewise, to those joining us from the former Ministry of Industrialization and Trade, I once again welcome you and assure you that your experience and skills are highly valued and appreciated in this new expanded structure. Let me emphasize that teamwork, collaboration, and adaptability are essential. All of us, regardless of our roles, are equally vital in this collective mission.” ; revealed that the political leadership of the ministry, together with management, would work closely with all departments and directorates to ensure a smooth transition over the coming days.

a3536.speaker: Selma Ashipala-Musavyi, Namibian Minister of International Relations and Trade
a3536.speech: “This transition is critical for fostering coordinated efforts in our economic diplomacy, with a strong focus on regional and continental integration through the African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA), as well as creating sustained economic relevance in the global economy through other international agreements.” ; said Namibia must focus on enhancing its trade capabilities through market diversification, concentrating on priority areas where comparative advantage exists: “We must prioritize key sectors such as agriculture, mining, renewable energy, and logistics, as well as trade in services, particularly tourism, business services, financial, health, transportation, and communication services, to position Namibia competitively within the African market.”

a3550.speaker: Bill Gates, co-chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation and co-founder of Microsoft
a3550.speech: Said Africa needs to achieve more, faster, and ensure everybody benefits as people tackle unemployment, malnutrition and health issues, emphasising the role of young people in finding new solutions: “We are the human beings who must take action, and we have to decide now, because this unique moment won’t last forever. We must clear away the obstacles that are standing in young people’s way so they can seize all of their potential.” ; “But our duty is not merely to arouse; our duty is to invest in young people, to put in place the basic building blocks so that they can build the future. And our duty is to do it now, because the innovations of tomorrow depend on the opportunities available to children today.” ; “What can South Africa be, what can Africa be, what can the world be – and what must we do to make it that way?” ; “It won’t be easy, but I believe it can be done. The successes and failures of the past 15 years have generated exemplars and lessons that we can learn from. Phenomenal advances in science and technology are constantly expanding the range of solutions available to solve development challenges. And then there is the ingenuity of the African people.”

a3550.speaker: Bill Gates, co-chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a3550.speech: Said Mandela was an “advisor and inspiration” while he was working on Aids issues on the continent, and said he learnt about the structural challenges needing to be tackled while at a community centre in Soweto which was running on a generator: “Computers alone can’t cure disease or feed children and if they can’t be turned on they can’t do much at all.”

a3550.speaker: Bill Gates, co-chair of the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation
a3550.speech: “African countries tend to have higher rates of inequality than countries on other continents. And despite healthy average GDP growth in the region, many countries have not shared in it. Gross inequalities exist both within countries and between countries. Until progress belongs to all people, everywhere, the real promise of living together will remain elusive.”

a3550.speaker: Forbes
a3550.speech: Puts Gates’ net worth at almost $80-billion, according to Forbes.

a3550.speaker: Thomas Piketty, French economist and author of Capital in the 21st Century
a3550.speech: Said stakeholders in Europe and America suffered from “historical amnesia” and were hypocritically preaching about good governance while not following their own advice on the continent ; “What Africa needs is not foreign aid. Africa is not asking for help. What Africa needs is an international legal system that allows African countries to make multinational companies and wealthy citizens pay their fair tax. This is what Europe and North America should now offer.” He called for international laws to be passed to prevent international companies evading taxes on the continent.

a3550.speaker: Professor Njabulo Ndebele, chairman of the board of the Nelson Mandela Foundation
a3550.speech: Noted the current challenges of inequality and questions about the disparity between the sacrifice and the fulfilment of a dream for the country: “Sometimes you can feel lost and even discarded. Then we ask how can we live together in dignity in the face of this gap?” ; “The dream of inclusion is swallowed up by the reality of exclusion.”

a3569.speaker: Nigeria Security Tracker (NST), database of the US foreign policy think-tank Council on Foreign Relations
a3569.speech: According to the NST, some 43,228 people were killed directly from the Boko Haram conflict in Nigeria between May 2011, when data collection started, and May 2023 when it closed.

a3569.speaker: Scott Perry, US congressman
a3569.speech: Alleging, in a viral video of a session of the US House of Representatives, that the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) had funded terrorist organisations during the Obama and Biden administrations; Perry specifically mentioned Boko Haram as one of the beneficiaries of USAID funding, alongside others such as the Taliban and ISIS.

a3569.speaker: Host of “Talk to Al Jazeera” (Al Jazeera journalist)
a3569.speech: “We have seen Boko Haram regroup, and regroup, and regroup. What is your answer to that? Do you have in some way fed the insurgents?” ; “What’s your suspicion?”

a3569.speaker: General Christopher Musa, Nigerian Chief of Defence Staff (CDS)
a3569.speech: “The problem is that, I think, we’ve talked to the international community. Let’s find out the funding…. As we speak, we have over 120,000 [Boko Haram members] that have surrendered. Most of them, when you find them, they are coming with hard currencies; how did they get them? How are they funded? How did they get the training? How did they get the equipment?” ; “Well, maybe an international conspiracy you don’t know, who knows? How are they able to sustain themselves for 15 years? That is one question I think everybody should ask themselves.”

a3569.speaker: Former presidents Muhammadu Buhari and Goodluck Jonathan
a3569.speech: Raised questions about certain aspects of the Boko Haram tragic story, and raised similar questions in the past about how Boko Haram has managed to remain resilient for so long.

a3569.speaker: Kashim Shettima, then governor of Borno State, now Nigerian Vice President
a3569.speech: Raised the concern about how come Boko Haram were better armed and motivated than Nigerian soldiers.

a3596.speaker: Bonifatius Wakudumo, Kavango East Governor
a3596.speech: criticized the organisers of the 'Men Commitment Walk' for failing to mobilise attendance. ; “I leave my title as governor, representing the president, and get in my own car, not the government's. I have to arrange for people to gather here, and without my efforts, this event would have flopped.” ; “You who are running these events come here and stand around; you don't mobilise people. What do you do? You just wait for attendees? How are people supposed to come to the meeting? I had to send my grandson in my own car to get this podium. This is in Rundu. Are we sabotaging this government, or what is happening? I have to be frank: we cannot work like this, colleagues.”

a3767.speaker: Berte Marie Ulveseter, Director of Norwegian Church Aid (NCA) Tanzania
a3767.speech: "This new strategy will focus on fighting inequality, eradicating gender-based violence, advancing the economy and food security, conserving the environment and responding to climate change." ; Said the strategy is built on NCA's commitment to just partnership and development led by the communities concerned, ensuring that communities are not merely recipients of aid but genuine participants in bringing about change.

a3767.speaker: Berte Marie Ulveseter, Director of Norwegian Church Aid (NCA) Tanzania
a3767.speech: "This is not just a strategy, but a call to action. We must continue to be attractive, to be relevant, and to have positive results. And above all, we must walk this journey together with communities, not on their behalf, in order to ensure just and sustainable results."

a3767.speaker: Berte Marie Ulveseter, Director of Norwegian Church Aid (NCA) Tanzania
a3767.speech: Describing the achievements of the previous five-year strategy, said that over 2020-2024 NCA and its partners delivered measurable achievements through inclusive, community-led and multi-faith projects, including more than 5,000 Inter-Religious Community Microfinance Groups; 24,976 women, men and young people receiving digital extension information and market opportunities through the JAMBOMAISHA platform; 27,023 people enabled to use innovative and environmentally friendly agricultural methods, technologies and services; 5,291 young people benefiting through agricultural innovation centres; 934 production groups established and formally registered with assured markets; 15,342 people receiving legal aid services; 83,747 women and girls reached with reproductive health and family planning education; more than 100 Public Expenditure Tracking committees established; and 40 inter-faith committees maintained at district and regional levels.

a3767.speaker: Berte Marie Ulveseter, Director of Norwegian Church Aid (NCA) Tanzania
a3767.speech: "All these achievements were made possible thanks to the partnerships we built with communities, civil society organisations, and especially our faith partners." ; "Christian and Muslim religious leaders have made a great contribution to advancing peace, health policies, tax justice, equality, and social change."

a3767.speaker: Norwegian Church Aid (NCA) Tanzania
a3767.speech: At this time when some donors are withdrawing, including USAID, extended its sincere thanks for the continued support from Norad and the people of Norway, who have continued to commit themselves to development and humanitarian work in Tanzania.

a4203.speaker: World Bank (official press release sent to Fratmat.info)
a4203.speech: States that this operation is intended to improve the profile of Ivorian debt and thereby free up funds for the implementation of projects in various sectors, including education: “This initiative, supported by the World Bank, will cover nearly 400 million euros of commercial debt, the most expensive held by Cote d’Ivoire, maturing over the next five years” ; stresses that the debt swap was made possible thanks to a policy-based guarantee estimated at 500 million euros (328,162,050,350 CFA francs) granted to Cote d’Ivoire, adding that about half of the guarantee will be used for the debt conversion and the remainder will allow the Ivorian government to obtain a sustainable-development-linked loan to broaden its investor base.

a4203.speaker: Anna Bjerde, World Bank Managing Director of Operations
a4203.speech: “Too many countries are facing rising debt-service payments that consume resources they could devote to development priorities such as education, preparing them for long-term success” ; “Through a pioneering conversion of debt in favour of development, facilitated by a World Bank guarantee, the government of Cote d’Ivoire aims to address both challenges at once. This innovative approach has strong potential for replication in other countries.”

a4203.speaker: Robert Beugre Mambe, Prime Minister of Cote d’Ivoire
a4203.speech: “Our government has applied a solid programme of reforms in fiscal consolidation, leading to sound debt management. We are proud to be the first country to implement the debt-for-development-programmes mechanism, based on the joint World Bank and IMF approach, to invest in human capital. In addition, we have used the World Bank Group’s guarantee platform to engage with environmental, social and governance investors through an innovative sustainable-development-linked loan. This pioneering approach reflects our commitment to exploring creative solutions that improve the well-being of our citizens while contributing to a healthier planet.”

a4385.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Minister of Finance and Development Planning
a4385.speech: Outlined progress made by the Boakai’s Administration for Liberia’s eligibility for the second Compact of the Millennium Challenge Corporation (MCC) ; cited the establishment and strengthening of an intra-governmental team focused on monitoring the MCC Scorecard to ensure Liberia meets the requirements ; informed the gathering that the Boakai’s Administration prioritizes transparency and accountability, highlighting ongoing efforts to hold individuals accused of corruption accountable, auditing ministries, agencies and commissions (MACs) and the formation of an assets recovery team, as key interventions made by the Liberian government.

a4385.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Minister of Finance and Development Planning
a4385.speech: Stressed the need to reinstate the US-Liberia Political Dialogue as a mechanism for strengthening relations between the two countries ; “The US-Liberia political dialogue is a structured framework for Liberia - America bilateral friendship,” he stated.

a4385.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Minister of Finance and Development Planning
a4385.speech: Reiterated the Liberian government’s dedication to accountability and improving the lives of its citizens ; added that the Liberia Anti-Corruption Commission and the General Auditing Commission are actively collaborating with the Ministry of Justice to prosecute those indicted in various reports.

a4385.speaker: Augustine Kpehe Ngafuan, Liberian Minister of Finance and Development Planning
a4385.speech: Highlighted Liberia’s constructive engagement with major international partners, citing recent achievements such as the approval of a US$210 million Economic Compact Fund (ECF) program by the IMF and US$60 million in direct budgetary support from the World Bank ; “These milestones reflect our commitment to meeting critical targets,” he noted.

a4385.speaker: Daniel W. Barnes, Managing Director of the Department of Policy and Evaluation Selection Eligibility and Policy Performance at the MCC
a4385.speech: Expressed gratitude to the Liberian delegation for their proactive engagement ; commended Liberia’s efforts in combating corruption and reducing poverty and pledged technical support for the intra-governmental committee focused on the MCC Scorecard.

a4385.speaker: Amy Holman, Acting Assistant Secretary for the Economic Bureau, US State Department
a4385.speech: Thanked the Minister and his delegation for the visit, and conveyed her impression of the level of work that is being done and expressed her commitment to working with the team.

a4385.speaker: Alexia Latortue, Assistant Secretary of the US Treasury Department on Fiscal Affairs
a4385.speech: Expressed the Treasury concern about the World Bank IDA replenishment and that Liberia is a good candidate for the pandemic resilience program ; assured the delegation of the US Treasury’s readiness to collaborate with the Government of Liberia on the reinstitution of the US-Liberia Political Dialogue, the support of the US CDC on the pandemic resilience program, and the preparedness of working with Liberia on her fiscal programs, policy on public private partnerships (PPP), infrastructure investment, capacity building.

a4474.speaker: USAID
a4474.speech: Said that the President's Malaria Initiative (PMI) project has been completed, and that under the four-year project more than 20 million insecticide-treated mosquito nets were distributed in Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar, protecting more than 35 million people.

a4474.speaker: Craig Hart, USAID Mission Director (public statement)
a4474.speech: Said they enabled the distribution of nets through campaigns in schools and health facilities, targeting at-risk groups such as infants and pregnant women: “The partnership between the United States and Tanzania spans more than six decades, and since 2006 PMI has invested more than 747 million dollars to combat malaria in Tanzania. We are proud of the achievements of the PMI project. Although this particular project has been completed, our commitment to working with the people of Tanzania to combat malaria and other community health challenges has not wavered.”

a4474.speaker: Naomi Serbantez, PMI Program Advisor in Tanzania
a4474.speech: Said that by building local expertise and using data-driven knowledge, the project has laid the foundation for sustainable progress in eliminating malaria across Mainland Tanzania and Zanzibar.

a4531.speaker: Hailu Assefa, member of the (Transmission Grid Code) Review Committee
a4531.speech: Said that though the Authority has finalised nearly the entire process for the Distribution Code, it is still working on the Transmission Code: “We want to table them for approval together. It’ll take another month to wrap up the inputs and get it finalised by consultants.”

a4531.speaker: Bahru Oljira, competency certification & technical regulation director at the Ethiopian Electric Authority
a4531.speech: Said the Code was supposed to be tabled for approval to the Authority in the last fiscal year, but the pandemic has slowed down the process: “Transmission and distribution are dealt with in different codes for simplicity.”

a4531.speaker: Mekdes Mezgebu, consultant and attorney at law at Mesfin Tafesse & Associates
a4531.speech: Said the Code has been eagerly anticipated for a long time and its formation will bring predictability to the playing field: “Private players will know what the requirements are to join the sector. This will, in turn, boost investor confidence.”

a4579.speaker: Domingos Estevao Fernandes, Permanent Representative of Mozambique to the United Nations
a4579.speech: Praised the support that the United Nations has provided to Mozambique, especially in efforts to stabilize the country, combat terrorism and provide humanitarian assistance ; highlighted the importance that Mozambique attributes to the UN, not only as the epicentre of global multilateralism, but also as a strategic partner in the country's development process.

a4579.speaker: Antonio Guterres, UN Secretary-General
a4579.speech: Praised Mozambique for its "exemplary performance" during its mandate as a non-permanent member of the Security Council, 2023-2024, highlighting the country's contribution to bringing together actors with opposing positions and to promoting international peace and security. He assured that the global organization will remain committed to mobilizing the international community to support Mozambique in combating terrorism and achieving the Sustainable Development Goals.

a4665.speaker: Kabir Shagaya, Director of Strategy for Cavista Holdings (parent company of Agbeyewa Farms)
a4665.speech: Explained that the 12-step plan builds on the successful signing of a Memorandum of Understanding between the company's chairman, Niyi John Olajide, and the Ekiti State Governor, Biodun Oyebanji, in May 2024 to establish a state-of-the-art cassava farm covering 100,000 hectares within the state ; “This programme is expected to impact 1,500 farmers across 10 cooperatives, benefiting approximately 7,500 individuals, including families, thereby supporting local communities and fostering economic growth and scalability” ; “Cassava has been overlooked as a staple crop in Nigeria; however, Agbeyewa Farms' long-term plan is to stimulate and ensure a cassava revolution that drives growth and prosperity in Nigeria.”

a4665.speaker: Kabir Shagaya, Director of Strategy for Cavista Holdings
a4665.speech: Revealed an investment plan for international donors, like USAID and the United States African Development Foundation (USADF), to join their program and support various aspects of their operations, such as farmer integration, infrastructure costs, initial operational needs, training, cooperative operations, and market integration through off-taker arrangements, all aimed at significantly reducing post-harvest losses.

a4665.speaker: Seyi Aiyeleso, Managing Director of Agbeyewa Farms
a4665.speech: Stated that the company is currently operating across 10,000 hectares of land across 9 communities in the state, and revealed that its 26-hectare agro-processing plant is set to commence operations soon and will produce high-quality cassava derivatives including flour, starch, and ethanol.

a4665.speaker: USAID Team (Xavier Preciado, Senior Agriculture Advisor; Susan Oranye, Project Management Specialist – Private Sector Engagement; Grace Bojuto, Manager/Executive Assistant to the Mission Director)
a4665.speech: Expressed their admiration for the high level of expertise, professionalism, and technology employed by the Agbeyewa team.

a4756.speaker: African First Ladies Peace Mission (AFLPM) in conjunction with the African Union (AU)
a4756.speech: Has called for more representation and inclusion of women in conflict management prevention and negotiation as a way of achieving sustainable peace in Africa.

a4756.speaker: Maria De Fatima Afonso Vila Nova, First Lady of the Republic of Sao Tome and Principe and Vice President of the African First Ladies Peace Mission
a4756.speech: Said that increasing women’s inclusion and voice would give the world a feeling of peace and the best chance of success ; “It is an honor to join women today in this important training program for women’s participation in conflict prevention, in this beautiful city of Abuja. Across the world, women are leading efforts for peace, justice, and rights, in a context of increasing conflict and climate disruption. Gender equality offers a path to sustainable peace and conflict prevention. In some countries, real progress in advancing women’s full, equal, and meaningful participation and involvement in efforts to achieve and maintain peace is being successful. And this is thanks to the strong leadership of national institutions, civil society organizations and individual women like all of us here today. With the adoption of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1325 (2000) on Women, Peace and Security (WPS) it announced a commitment by governments to recognize and fully support the full and equitable role that women play in preventing and resolving armed conflicts, peacekeeping, post-conflict reconstruction and humanitarian assistance, and in all efforts to promote peace and security at local, national and international levels. However, while the global WPS agenda has progressed and evolved over the past 24 years, the world it has not become a more peaceful or safe place – especially for women.”

a4756.speaker: Nadia Roguiai, Gender, Peace and Security Coordinator, African Union Commission, Political Affairs Peace and Security Department
a4756.speech: Said women have been excluded from the formal processes of peacebuilding and diplomacy for so long and there is a need to address it ; “As we stand at the crossroads of a rapidly changing world geopolitical conflicts, social and humanitarian crises shape our daily lives we are constantly challenged to find new and innovative ways to prevent violence, resolve disputes, and build lasting peace. These challenges are great, but they are not insurmountable. One of the most powerful, yet often overlooked, solutions lies in unlocking the full potential of women, particularly in the realms of mediation and preventive diplomacy.” ; “Despite the overwhelming evidence of their positive impact, women remain significantly underrepresented in key leadership positions within diplomacy and peacebuilding. Globally, women make up only a small fraction of mediators and negotiators. This systemic underrepresentation is not merely an issue of fairness; it is a missed opportunity for lasting, comprehensive peace. We have the knowledge, the experience, and the tools to create a world where women play an equal and central role in the pursuit of peace. But it requires a collective, sustained effort from all of us. Governments, international organizations, regional bodies, and civil society must work together to dismantle the barriers that prevent women from taking leadership roles. We must ensure that women’s contributions to peacebuilding are valued, amplified, and integrated into all decision-making processes” ; stressed the need to harness the full potential of women in diplomacy and peacebuilding by investing in the capacity of women leaders and civil society organizations.

a4756.speaker: Veronica Sesay, President of ECOFEPA (represented by Maimouna Ceesay)
a4756.speech: Noted that conflict prevention demands constant vigilance, thoughtful care, and proactive measures to address issues before they escalate into violence ; “The essence of conflict prevention is akin to nurturing a garden. It demands constant vigilance, thoughtful care, and proactive measures to address issues before they escalate into violence. By identifying potential sources of conflict early and addressing them through inclusive policies and sustainable development efforts, we can prevent violence and foster a stable, just, and peaceful society. This requires us to address the root causes of conflict, such as poverty, inequality, and political instability, with empathy and unwavering commitment.”

a4775.speaker: Shein customers on social media
a4775.speech: Across social media platforms, customers are reporting a sudden sharp increase in customs tax.

a4775.speaker: Clivia Arendse, regular Shein shopper
a4775.speech: Told News24 that her most recent package weighed about 0.0353kg and she paid R322.65 in customs, but previously she paid only R135 for a similar package.

a4775.speaker: Another Shein client (unnamed)
a4775.speech: Reported that she received a bill for taxes of more than R777 on a R2 400 order.

a4775.speaker: SA Revenue Service (SARS) spokesperson
a4775.speech: Said the agency is not aware of any increase in customs duties ; SARS also pointed out that clearing agents that receive the imports levy charge a service fee in addition to the customs duties.

a4775.speaker: SA Revenue Service (SARS)
a4775.speech: SARS did not respond to a query about whether it increased its scrutiny of Shein imports amid a South African government probe into the exporter's customs duty compliance.

a4775.speaker: Ebrahim Patel, Trade, Industry and Competition Minister
a4775.speech: Told News24 that clothing importers must pay 45% in duties, but that Shein seems to believe its imports are entitled to a much lower duty; said lower duties are meant for small quantities of imported clothing – like a single specialist wedding dress: “Shein, of course, is an industrial-scale operation bringing in huge quantities of clothing but packages in small amounts.” ; Added that Shein was using the lower duty in ways it was not intended, which is creating an “unfair playing field” and could result in massive job losses in the local clothing industry.

a4775.speaker: Shein
a4775.speech: Previously told News24 that the company was committed to adhering to local laws and regulations in all its markets.

a4775.speaker: Buffalo International Logistics
a4775.speech: The company told News24 that it is aware of the social media discussion about custom duties.

a4775.speaker: Travis Haefele, Buffalo International Logistics spokesperson
a4775.speech: Said the group had launched an internal probe to address any concerns related to changes in customs duties “due to system glitches or business adjustments”.

a4775.speaker: Clivia Arendse, regular Shein shopper
a4775.speech: Told News24 she preferred Shein to local clothing retailers because of its inclusive clothing size range and cheaper products: “When you go to normal stores, you really struggle to find what you want, and the clothing that is available for smaller sizes is usually not available for larger sizes”; but she says the hike in custom duties may dissuade her from purchasing from Shein in future.

a4775.speaker: Shein
a4775.speech: The company told News24 that its suppliers must adhere to a strict code of conduct according to the International Labour Organisation core conventions; as for the environmental concerns raised, it claims its model was especially good at reducing wastage, because it avoids overproduction due to its on-demand model.

a4913.speaker: US government
a4913.speech: Passed a law demanding the app's sale or ban because of what it says are its links to the Chinese state.

a4913.speaker: TikTok and its parent company ByteDance
a4913.speech: Deny the alleged links to the Chinese state ; TikTok has asked a court for an emergency injunction to prevent it becoming unavailable in the US next month, and said after losing its appeal that it would appeal to the Supreme Court.

a4913.speaker: Department of Justice (DOJ)
a4913.speech: Has called for the request to be dismissed, saying its underlying arguments have already been “definitively rejected.”

a4913.speaker: ByteDance and TikTok (emergency legal filing)
a4913.speech: Say an injunction is also justified because Donald Trump is about to replace Joe Biden as president. “The public interest favours providing sufficient time for the Supreme Court to conduct an orderly review process, and for the incoming Administration to evaluate this exceptionally important case” ; added that even a temporary ban from early 2025 would have “devastating effects” on its operations and would be “inflicting irreparable injury by silencing Petitioners and the 170 million Americans who use the platform each month” ; also said that even a temporary ban could cause a loss of revenue, as well as a loss of users and creators.

a4913.speaker: Judges of the appeals court
a4913.speech: On Friday, judges rejected the idea that the law was unconstitutional – saying it was the result of “extensive, bipartisan action” by lawmakers. They further concluded the law was “carefully crafted to deal only with control by a foreign adversary, and it was part of a broader effort to counter a well-substantiated national security threat posed by the PRC (People's Republic of China).”

a4913.speaker: TikTok's lawyers
a4913.speech: In Monday's request for an emergency injunction, argued the law would “inflict extreme and irreparable harm” on the company – adding it would do so “on the eve of a presidential inauguration”.

a4913.speaker: Donald Trump, US President-elect
a4913.speech: Has previously indicated he would overturn the law and has previously claimed he would “save TikTok” from a ban ; ahead of the run-up to the November election, Trump said the law would benefit Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram.

a4913.speaker: Experts (unnamed)
a4913.speech: Have warned that while Trump's promises may offer a lifeline for the company's US future, they are no guarantee of the action he will take once in office.

a4913.speaker: DOJ officials
a4913.speech: Said in their letter also filed on Monday that the appeals court should reject the injunction request. “The Court is familiar with the relevant facts and law and has definitively rejected petitioners' constitutional claims in a thorough decision that recognizes the critical national-security interests underlying the Act,” they argue.

a5210.speaker: World Health Organization (WHO)
a5210.speech: Has warned that South Sudan is among 8 countries in the world to run out of Antiretroviral therapy drugs in the coming month due to disruption on the global HIV programme.

a5210.speaker: Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO chief
a5210.speech: Said 8 countries globally including South Sudan are facing substantial consequence of the US cessation on funding to foreign countries ; said the disruption in HIV program could undo 20 years of progress which would lead to potential rise in prevalence and fatality.

a5210.speaker: Dr. Meg Doherty, WHO global director of HIV, Hepatitis and Sexually Transmitted Disease
a5210.speech: Said six of the eight are African countries of Kenya, Nigeria, Burkina Faso, Mali, Lesotho and South Sudan, with Haiti and war-torn Ukraine also reported to face a similar HIV shortage; stated that these countries are already at risk of other outbreaks, infections and emergencies that challenges their health sectors: “Currently, the countries we are most worried about are countries you would know have been at risk of other outbreaks, infections and emergencies including Haiti, Kenya Lesotho, South Sudan, Burkina Fasso, Mali, Nigeria and Ukraine.” ; “We are working with team to see how we can avert the challenges in future. Next week things might be different.” She underscored that the global health agency and partners are working closely with a team to ensure the HIV program shock in these countries are averted.

a5210.speaker: National Empowerment of Positive Women United (NEPWU), non-profit working with people living with HIV in South Sudan
a5210.speech: Revealed in February 2025 that around 70,000 people have been directly affected by Donald Trump's 90-day suspension of U.S. foreign aid.

a5210.speaker: Mama Evelyn Letio, Executive Director of the National Empowerment of Positive Women United (NEPWU)
a5210.speech: Said the PEPFAR program used to donate $1 million annually to the organization and accounted for 75% of the organization's budget; revealed that within an estimated number of nearly 200,000 people living with HIV in South Sudan, nearly 70,000 rely on international assistance; and said the suspension threatens to reverse years of momentum gained in fighting the pandemic.

a5212.speaker: Shimizu Fumio, Ambassador of Japan to Eswatini
a5212.speech: In his speech, expressed his enthusiasm for participating in this pivotal event, underscoring Japan's long-standing commitment to supporting the people of Eswatini. He stated, “This support aligns with Japan's mission to eradicate hunger and malnutrition, enabling vulnerable children to pursue their dreams.”

a5212.speaker: Dr. Tambo Gina, Minister of Economic Planning and Development of Eswatini
a5212.speech: Expressed heartfelt gratitude for Japan's unwavering support; he highlighted how this initiative aligns with Eswatini's National Development Plan (NDP) 2023/24 – 2027/28, emphasising the shared vision of reducing poverty and improving the quality of life for all citizens.

a5212.speaker: Ministry of Economic Planning and Development of Eswatini
a5212.speech: Extended heartfelt thanks to the Government of Japan for its generous support, which is expected to have a lasting impact on the lives of thousands of children in Eswatini.

a5352.speaker: Saul Bellow, 1915-2005, writer
a5352.speech: “Power and money of course do drive people crazy. So, why shouldn’t people gain power and wealth through being crazy?” ; “Having power destroys the sanity of the powerful. It allows their irrationalities to leave the sphere of the dream and come into the real world”.

a5352.speaker: Lord Acton, 1834-1902
a5352.speech: “Power tends to corrupt; and absolute power corrupts absolutely. Great men are almost always bad men”.

a5352.speaker: Euripides, 480-406 BC
a5352.speech: “Those whom God wishes to destroy, he first makes mad.”

a5352.speaker: William Sherden, in Best Laid Plans: The Tyranny of Unintended Consequences and How To Avoid Them
a5352.speech: “Sometimes unintended consequences are catastrophic, sometimes beneficial. Occasionally, their impacts are imperceptible, at other times colossal.”

a5405.speaker: Gabriel Hanotaux, French historian and politician
a5405.speech: Wrote: "Whoever possesses the Red Sea possesses the world."

a5405.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti
a5405.speech: Wrote when presenting the "Djibouti Vision 2035" development plan: "Knowing where one wants to go is all very well. One still has to show that one is going there." ; also said "one must know where one comes from."

a5405.speaker: Ayeid Mousseid Yahya, Ambassador of Djibouti to France
a5405.speech: Said that at independence Djibouti was a "bare rock" and that in 45 years it has been made into "something that resonates beyond the borders of the Republic of Djibouti"; explained that since President Omar Guelleh came to power in 1999 Djibouti has "changed its face": the city has been structurally transformed, the country has developed its ports to seven today, the Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway has been rebuilt as a double-track electric line, "the first of its kind in Africa", Djibouti is among the few sub-Saharan African countries carrying out water desalination, power cuts have been addressed through interconnections with Ethiopia and a wind farm at Goubet built with a Spanish company, two solar fields are to be built in the north with French industrialists, and geothermal energy is being developed with the first kilowatts expected in coming years ; said growth takes time, that the population has grown from 450,000-500,000 at independence to one million, that the country went from a single secondary school to around forty and from a few doctors to thousands, as the fruit of growth and "the fair redistribution of the wealth created", with growth often approaching 7% over the last ten years and today of the order of 3.5% owing to global disturbances.

a5405.speaker: Ayeid Mousseid Yahya, Ambassador of Djibouti to France
a5405.speech: Said "Djibouti is a tourist country with incredible sites," but that the country fears mass tourism and seeks to develop tourist infrastructure while respecting and protecting nature, noting the growth from a single high-end hotel, the Sheraton, to a plethora including the Kempinski Palace, with the Accor group soon opening two more ; said that for agriculture the great concern was water availability and that now the sector is developing, with market gardening in which "the role of women is preponderant" soon able to satisfy nearly 50% of local demand ; said Djibouti prefers to preserve and develop traditional rather than industrial fishing to protect its seabeds, with the authorities granting aid and guarantees to fishermen and subsidising diesel, and that the whale shark site should be turned into a sanctuary and preserved.

a5405.speaker: Ayeid Mousseid Yahya, Ambassador of Djibouti to France
a5405.speech: Said unemployment is "this thorn in our foot", especially youth unemployment, attributing it partly to a country that "has acquired the reflexes of the French administration" with a tendency to prefer the civil service to the private sector or entrepreneurship; said reforms have been adopted to push young people towards more voluntarism, notably the establishment of the Investment Guarantee Fund, and that the government has the question at heart but cannot resolve it alone, while remaining attentive to industrial sectors developing in the free zones.

a5405.speaker: Ayeid Mousseid Yahya, Ambassador of Djibouti to France
a5405.speech: Said that where each large group such as Djibouti Telecom or Electricite de Djibouti previously had its own fund, Djibouti now has a sovereign wealth fund bringing together all the profits, which supports company creation and job creation; said the country has a very attractive investment code offering exemptions from taxes and duties during the first five years depending on the initial investment, which has allowed Turkish, Saudi, Chinese and other foreign companies to set up.

a5405.speaker: Ayeid Mousseid Yahya, Ambassador of Djibouti to France
a5405.speech: Said French companies "had lost the taste for adventure" and that this is a great pity, but that things are changing since the arrival of President Emmanuel Macron; said European countries face competition across Africa from companies from elsewhere and must be competitive and think in terms of win-win, long-term investments rather than market share alone, noting that Djibouti is a gateway to other COMESA countries such as Ethiopia and South Sudan and that returns on investment can come quickly; said the President of Djibouti has always invited French companies "not to miss the train" and that they will always be welcome, but that Italian, Emirati, Turkish and other companies came to take the empty place because "nature abhors a vacuum", citing Bred, the only French bank in Djibouti, as having found its place and even a foot in the Ethiopian market.

a5405.speaker: International Monetary Fund (IMF)
a5405.speech: According to the IMF, debt service could reach 5% of Djibouti's GDP this year.

a5405.speaker: Ayeid Mousseid Yahya, Ambassador of Djibouti to France
a5405.speech: Said only two investments required Chinese loans - water production and the Addis Ababa-Djibouti railway line - and that the railway will generate profits and repay its own construction, while the water investment was fundamental because water is a scarce commodity, with Chinese investment allowing Djibouti to fetch water 250 kilometres away; said Chinese loans in Djibouti's projects "are never in the majority" and will be repaid, as credits were repaid for the container port built with Emirati partners, which has belonged to Djibouti ever since; said "Name me a single country that developed without credit. Not even the United States. We know exactly what is good for Djibouti, and we will never do anything that could one day harm our national sovereignty," adding that the fear stirred up "here and there" is "in reality a pressure between the powerful, and we are the victims."

a5405.speaker: Ismail Omar Guelleh, President of Djibouti
a5405.speech: Commented in an interview with Jeune Afrique in November 2020: "Paris should become aware that Djibouti's interest is not only geostrategic. It is also geo-economic."

a5405.speaker: Ayeid Mousseid Yahya, Ambassador of Djibouti to France
a5405.speech: On France-Djibouti relations, said Djibouti is the country in the Horn of Africa that has always been at peace and has not known war, that the presence of armed forces makes the country safer, but that France "must ask itself whether it has not missed something in Djibouti and correct its aim"; granted that things are moving since the arrival of President Macron, who saw for himself during his visit what the "bare rock" has become; said Djibouti has undertaken reforms to attract foreign and especially French investors, that the Embassy in Paris is an active member of the Franco-Arab Chamber of Commerce, that French companies are once again interested but there remains "this prism of a France that has lost the taste for adventure", that French investments must match the ambitions of the two heads of state, and cited a new study for the construction of a new airport to be financed with a concessional loan from France.

a5405.speaker: Ayeid Mousseid Yahya, Ambassador of Djibouti to France
a5405.speech: Said the Franco-Arab Chamber of Commerce (CCFA) has already played this role in the past, having organised a breakfast-debate in honour of the President of Djibouti during his 2012 visit to France; hoped that President Reina would relaunch the initiative blocked by Covid-19 to accompany a group of business leaders to Djibouti, and said the CCFA can be the catalyst for SMEs wanting to establish themselves in Djibouti to access the Djiboutian market and a regional market of 400 million consumers, encouraging it to go in that direction.

a5520.speaker: Uba Sani, Kaduna State Governor (represented by the Secretary to the Kaduna State Government, Dr AbdulKadir Muazu Meyere)
a5520.speech: Promised that his administration will improve the livestock industry, bridge infrastructure deficit, facilitate access to markets and attract investment ; disclosed that Arla Farms has invested 10 million Euros to establish state-of-the-art Arla Farms in Damau Household Milk Farm located at Kubau local government area in 2023 ; said that Arla Farms targets “a 4–5 million kg milk output target at full capacity annually” ; said there has been a boost in local milk production as well as the creation of local direct and indirect jobs at Arla Farms since his administration came on board.

a5520.speaker: Uba Sani, Kaduna State Governor
a5520.speech: Recalled that his Government has instituted a strong institutional framework to ensure the sustainability, expansion and investment in the agricultural sector: “In the livestock subsector, Kaduna State has the Kaduna State Livestock Regulatory Authority (KADLRA), the Kaduna State Livestock Transformation Company, and the Kaduna Ranch Development Company, all of which are designed to work in synergy.”

a5520.speaker: Uba Sani, Kaduna State Governor
a5520.speech: Expressed delight to be part of the unveiling of “the Nigeria Dairy Center of Excellence, the Sedentarization and Climate change Resilience in Nigeria (SCREEN) Project, as well as commissioning of a yoghurt factory” ; said the initiatives will complement the efforts of his administration in empowering smallholder farmers by equipping them with modern techniques and technologies to improve milk yield and quality as well as supporting local milk sourcing “which translates into more income for our farmers, more jobs for our youth, and more nutritious products for our people” ; “We hope that the multistakeholder collaboration that birthed the Damau Milk Farm Project will not only help in revamping the project but also galvanize sustainable economic growth in the dairy value chain in Nigeria, with Kaduna State in the lead.”

a5520.speaker: Idi Mukhtar Maiha, Minister of Livestock Development (representing President Bola Tinubu)
a5520.speech: Noted that the Arla Farm is a result of the Federal Government’s policy on local content development/backward integration; commended the officials of the Federal Government, the Kaduna State Government, and Arla for this win-win initiative.

a5520.speaker: Idi Mukhtar Maiha, Minister of Livestock Development
a5520.speech: Lamented that Nigeria currently produces only about 0.7 million litres of milk annually, which is far below the amount required to meet the nutritional needs of its population ; “Our average per capita consumption of 8.7 million litres of milk per year is not only well below the global average but also alarmingly lower than the World Health Organisation’s recommended intake of 210 litres per person annually.” ; “At the farm level, the productivity gap is just as stark; the average milk yield of our indigenous cows is only 0.5 to 1.5 litres per day, compared to the global average of 6.6 litres.” ; “Furthermore, the country spends over $1.5 billion annually importing milk and dairy products, despite having millions of cattle and capable producers. This is a paradox that we must correct.”

a5520.speaker: Idi Mukhtar Maiha, Minister of Livestock Development
a5520.speech: Said the Ministry of Livestock Development was established to unlock the potential of Nigeria’s livestock value chains, reduce dependence on imports, mitigate farmer-herder conflicts, and ensure nutrition and prosperity for citizens: “Today, that vision is taking shape through investments such as the Arla Farm, as well as collaborations and reforms that are already yielding results.”

a5520.speaker: Idi Mukhtar Maiha, Minister of Livestock Development
a5520.speech: Noted that “the Damau area is becoming the dairy hub of Nigeria, thanks to its key dairy interventions, including the Arla Farm, owned by Arla, the Damau Household Milk Farm, and the Dairy Development projects” ; explained that the Damau Household Milk Farm, initiated by the Kaduna State Government, is being implemented in collaboration with investors and development partners, involving “the settlement of 1,000 households and the provision of basic production items, such as improved cows, pasture, veterinary services, and other social amenities” ; “Arla serves as the off-taker of milk from the cows. To ensure resounding success, the Danish Government is sponsoring two dairy development projects that are building the capacity of local producers and improving their livelihoods.”

a5686.speaker: Economists
a5686.speech: Argued that the [2008 Omitara-Otjivero BIG] pilot was too small-scale and short-term to assess the long-term economic impacts.

a5686.speaker: Namibian gender ministry
a5686.speech: Late last year announced the conversion of the Food Bank Programme and Marginalised Communities Special Feeding initiative into a monthly household cash payout of N$600 ; according to the ministry, 8 238 households currently receive the BIG payout nationwide.

a5686.speaker: Data collected in 2023
a5686.speech: Revealed that approximately 12 699 additional households qualify for registration.

a5969.speaker: Government of Ghana
a5969.speech: In January 2025, Ghana announced the creation of the Gold Board (whose launch is planned for March 2025), which will centralise gold production from small- and large-scale mining projects for international exports ; in August 2024, Ghana also unveiled its draft mining cooperation policy aimed at establishing community mining cooperatives.

a6144.speaker: US Government led by Donald Trump
a6144.speech: Confirmed this week that it will eliminate more than 90% of the foreign aid contracts of the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) and 60 billion dollars (58 billion euros) in general assistance worldwide.

a6144.speaker: Paul Nantulya, researcher at the Africa Center for Strategic Studies
a6144.speech: “Among African leaders, China has already built significant influence. Now it has the opportunity to seduce public opinion,” he explained ; “China is using every tool at its disposal to obtain this competitive advantage over the United States,” the researcher described ; “Right now, I bet that in Beijing officials are studying the next step and when and how to increase China's contribution,” he pointed out.

a6144.speaker: Paul Nantulya, researcher at the Africa Center for Strategic Studies
a6144.speech: “When the West withheld donations of vaccines and medical equipment, China quickly filled the vacuum,” Nantulya recalled. “In exchange, they received a lot of publicity and prestige, for a relatively small investment,” he observed.

a6144.speaker: International Futures, University of Denver (analysis)
a6144.speech: An analysis carried out by International Futures, at the University of Denver, concluded that the cuts could push a further 5.7 million Africans below the extreme poverty line of 2.15 dollars a day in the coming year.

a6144.speaker: Gallup Association (international poll)
a6144.speech: According to an international poll by the Gallup Association, Beijing's approval among Africans went from 52% in 2022 to 58% in 2023, while Washington's popularity fell from 59% to 56% in the same period.

a6144.speaker: Afrobarometer and the Ichikowitz Family Foundation (surveys)
a6144.speech: Surveys conducted by other institutes, such as Afrobarometer and the Ichikowitz Family Foundation, demonstrate the same trend (that China has overtaken the United States in popularity among African public opinion).

a6147.speaker: Hussein Bashe, Tanzanian Agriculture Minister
a6147.speech: Has given Pretoria and Lilongwe until Wednesday next week to remove non-tariff barriers on Tanzanian produce or it will restrict all farming imports from the countries, he said in a post on X ; Farm goods from the two nations wouldn't be allowed to transit through Tanzania or its ports, Bashe said. Additionally, the country would block shipments of fertilizer to Malawi, he said.

a6175.speaker: Donald Trump, President of the United States
a6175.speech: Decided to suspend foreign development aid for 90 days in order, according to him, to assess the effectiveness of the programmes and their alignment with American foreign policy ; argues that this aid "is not aligned with American interests and, in many cases, is contrary to American values."

a6175.speaker: Edouard T. Diapa, president of the community convergence network of Faso (COCOFA) and president of the coalition of networks and associations for the fight against HIV/AIDS and health promotion (CORAB)
a6175.speech: Said it is an unprecedented crisis with regard to the care of vulnerable populations ; explained that for several years community-based organisations in Burkina Faso have played a crucial role in medical care, prevention and protection of vulnerable populations, notably through projects financed by USAID and PEPFAR, and that these programmes ensure access to care, treatment and essential social services for thousands of people, in particular people living with HIV ; said the reassessment and realignment of USAID funding has led to the suspension of access to vital services for hundreds, even thousands of beneficiaries, which is worrying ; said the situation seems like the state being abandoned mid-flight by its partners, a state already making great budgetary efforts in the fight against terrorism ; wondered how Burkina will continue to ensure the care of patients on antiretrovirals, medical care and the payment of the personnel who look after them, given that its American partner is abandoning ship without warning ; "I believe it is a loss for the beneficiaries, for the Burkinabe state through the Permanent Secretariat for the Fight against HIV/AIDS and STIs (SP CNLS-IST). PEPFAR provides enormous support for the fight against HIV in Burkina Faso." ; is convinced that the shock wave of this funding cut will be felt at all levels of the fight against HIV, though he hopes everything will resume after the three-month suspension, even if the indicators do not bode well.

a6175.speaker: Edouard T. Diapa, president of COCOFA
a6175.speech: On self-reliance: said this is proof that when you sleep on someone else's mat, you sleep on the ground. "That is also why I believe our state is right to say that we must work towards being truly independent. It is now that everyone must become aware that each person must work and realise that our government has a good vision. We must support them whatever happens."

a6175.speaker: Edouard T. Diapa, president of COCOFA
a6175.speech: Pleaded for the return of American aid, which greatly relieves the Burkinabe state: "Finally, I make an appeal to the American people, who have always remained faithful to the Burkinabe people despite the difficulties Burkina Faso has been going through in terms of security, as have other peoples, namely the Dutch people, etc. I tell them that good friends do not abandon each other in times of difficulty."

a6175.speaker: UNAIDS
a6175.speech: Gives assurances (as reported by Diapa) that there is no break in funding for antiretrovirals, the medicines that HIV patients take continuously.

a6527.speaker: Benin government (unnamed officials, reported rhetoric)
a6527.speech: “Tighten your belts; within a year or two the people will see the social benefits of the government's action programme” — described as soothing words served up to the population to ease their suffering, at least psychologically.

a6527.speaker: Government of Benin
a6527.speech: As early as November 2016, announced the end of the occupation of public thoroughfares for commercial activities and other services.

a6527.speaker: Government Action Programme (Programme d'action du gouvernement)
a6527.speech: Pledges the creation, in time, of 600,000 jobs.

a6556.speaker: Ibrahim Toure, author and Ambassador of Cote d'Ivoire to the United States
a6556.speech: Taking the floor, expressed his gratitude to the authorities present, to his academic and professional mentors, as well as to his family. He explained that "The Shadow and the Prey" was born of a childhood dream, nourished over the years by a desire to take a critical look at current problems such as cybercrime and illegal immigration.

a6556.speaker: Leon Kacou Adom, Minister (of Foreign Affairs of Cote d'Ivoire)
a6556.speech: In his address, praised the human and professional qualities of his collaborator, while discovering in him an unsuspected literary talent. He congratulated the author for the richness of the content and for the contribution of his work to Ivorian literature.

a6556.speaker: Tene Birahima Ouattara, Minister of State, Minister of Defence, author of the book's preface
a6556.speech: Underlined the relevance of the themes addressed, which concern society as a whole. He also appreciated the fluid and accessible style of the work, which facilitates its reading and comprehension.

a6634.speaker: UN representatives
a6634.speech: According to UN representatives, in the east of the DRC the quest for peace remains difficult, but not impossible.

a6634.speaker: Bintou Keita, UN Special Envoy and head of MONUSCO
a6634.speech: Reported on Monday in New York on the progress made in the search for peace in the east of the DRC; before the Security Council, stated that fighting persists between the Congolese army and rebel groups such as the M23, backed by Rwanda, while stressing the persistence of mineral trafficking and sexual violence in the region ; «Peace has not yet been won», she warned, while welcoming the notable reduction in fighting since the announcement of a ceasefire on 30 July between the DRC and Rwanda ; «There is today an active framework of dialogue between the DRC and Rwanda, and a real prospect of peace can therefore be envisaged.»

a6634.speaker: Bintou Keita, UN Special Envoy and head of MONUSCO
a6634.speech: Also mentioned the progress made in the political and budgetary processes in the DRC, enabling the government of Prime Minister Judith Suminwa to implement its programme.

a6634.speaker: Bintou Keita, UN Special Envoy and head of MONUSCO
a6634.speech: Recalled the disbursement of more than one billion dollars in humanitarian aid; however, the funding expected this year will remain below the some 2.6 billion dollars needed to assist the 8.7 million most vulnerable people in 2024.

a6634.speaker: Bintou Keita, UN Special Envoy and head of MONUSCO
a6634.speech: Added that the neutralisation of the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF), a rebel group affiliated with the jihadist organisation Islamic State since 2019, in North Kivu and Ituri, remains «a priority» of MONUSCO, after a record 272 civilians were killed by this group last June.

a6634.speaker: Bintou Keita, UN Special Envoy and head of MONUSCO
a6634.speech: Assured that the protection of civilians remains a priority for the UN troops, stating that the interventions of the Blue Helmets in Ituri and North Kivu are «more agile and robust».

a6750.speaker: Draft resolution of the emergency Arab-Islamic summit (seen by Reuters)
a6750.speech: Condemns what it calls Israel's "hostile acts including genocide, ethnic cleansing, [and] starvation", which it says threatens "prospects of peace and coexistence".

a6750.speaker: Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim al-Thani, Qatari Prime Minister
a6750.speech: Urged the international community to stop applying "double standards" and to punish Israel.

a6750.speaker: Donald Trump, US President
a6750.speech: Said that "Qatar has been a very great ally. ... Israel and everybody else, we have to be careful. When we attack people we have to be careful."

a6750.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a6750.speech: Departing for Israel on Saturday, said Trump "didn't like the way [the Qatar attack] went down".

a6750.speaker: UN Security Council (statement)
a6750.speech: Condemned the Israeli strike on Qatar's capital: "Council members underscored the importance of de-escalation and expressed their solidarity with Qatar," the 15-member council said in a statement.

a6750.speaker: Isaac Herzog, Israeli President
a6750.speech: Defended Israel's action, saying that the strike was necessary to "remove some of the people if they are not willing to get a deal" to end the war.

a6750.speaker: Hamas
a6750.speech: Said its negotiating team survived the Israeli strike on 9 September - but five of its members were killed, including the son of the group's chief negotiator Khalil al-Hayya.

a6871.speaker: Kelly Stone, researcher (author of the study/article)
a6871.speech: indicated in the article that the interruption of USAID funding, imposed by US President Donald Trump, could increase the risk of human rights violations and reduce citizens' trust in their governments, leaving countries more vulnerable to even more violent extremism ; “Terrorist groups frequently exploit low levels of citizen trust, abuses by the security forces, and underlying poverty and exclusion as their main recruitment instruments. The potential consequences are alarming, especially in the countries of West Africa, Somalia and Mozambique, where violent extremist groups cause widespread violence.”

a6871.speaker: Kelly Stone, researcher (author of the study/article)
a6871.speech: gave as an example that in 2024 programmes supporting democracy, human rights, governance and security represented 10% of the aid package for Africa proposed by USAID, worth eight billion dollars ; “The main beneficiaries of non-humanitarian US aid were Nigeria (600 million euros), Mozambique (544 million euros), Tanzania (540 million euros), Uganda (539 million euros) and Kenya (494 million euros).” ; stressed that in 2022 all African countries received US aid in some form, varying between 125 million and 500 million dollars, and that “a total or partial withdrawal would harm economic progress and exacerbate poverty, worsening humanitarian crises.”

a6871.speaker: Kelly Stone, researcher (author of the study/article)
a6871.speech: said the cessation of aid to Africa “could create a vacuum that rebels could exploit and could compromise security”, but could also increase the influence of authoritarian regimes - such as China and Russia - on the continent ; warned that “this could restrict US access to emerging markets, leading to the loss of commercial opportunities in a region full of potential and promoting the development of policies that run counter to US interests” ; underlined that Trump's current policy sees this type of foreign aid as “an unnecessary expense” ; said the abandonment of the US role in Africa would interrupt vital development initiatives, worsen instability and poverty and disturb geopolitical alignments ; criticised: “Considering that Trump did not visit Africa a single time during his first term and made disparaging statements about the continent, his ignorance about Africa is not surprising.”

a6871.speaker: Marco Rubio, US Secretary of State
a6871.speech: accused USAID of being “completely devoid of any capacity to respond”, criticising the “insubordination” in that body.

a6883.speaker: One writer (unnamed)
a6883.speech: Aptly observes that Nigeria imports toothpicks despite having bamboo; starch even though it is the world’s largest cassava producer; and tomatoes while having its own tomato production base.

a6883.speaker: Aliko Dangote / Dangote (Dangote Petroleum Refinery and Petrochemicals)
a6883.speech: Proudly declared on Tuesday: “We are committed to ensuring that starting in October, there will be no need to import polypropylene. Our petrochemical plant will be fully capable of meeting all local demands”.

a6883.speaker: Depot and Petroleum Products Marketers Association of Nigeria (DAPPMAN) (letter to President Bola Tinubu)
a6883.speech: Expressed worries about financial losses incurred by its members due to Dangote Refinery’s decision to reduce the price of Automotive Gas Oil (diesel) from N1,700 to N900 upon starting production in January. The association said that players in the downstream petroleum sector have invested over N3 trillion in establishing around 130 private petroleum depots.

a7075.speaker: Australasia's Mining Weekly (report)
a7075.speech: Reported that the Mining Development Agreement (MDA) the government signed with Lotus Resources in July 2024 guarantees a stability period of 10 years during which the project will not be subject to any detrimental changes to the fiscal regime: “Key tax terms are aligned with the restart definitive feasibility study assumptions, including a royalty rate of 5% and a corporate tax rate of 30%” ; “Relief is provided on resource rental tax and withholding tax, specifically as it applies to dividends to non-residents. There are exemptions for import and duties, excise and value-added tax on capital goods and specified consumables directly related to mine production. The MDA includes internationally recognised principles relating to legal protection on security of tenure, dispute resolution and expropriation.”

a7075.speaker: Chifipa Mhango, Chief Economist, Don Consultancy Group (South Africa)
a7075.speech: Observed that the historical nature of the July 2024 Kayelekera Mine deal is a clear demonstration that Malawi's economic authorities need to solidify and beef up their negotiation efforts in mining deals: “We continue to make the same mistakes with no sense of correction” ; “The recent negotiations and process leading to the signing of the new Mine Development Agreement of July 31, 2024, presented an opportunity to rectify the past mistakes.” ; added that in its report of June 2015 ActionAid described as harmful the tax breaks granted to foreign multinational mining companies in Malawi, such as that given to Paladin (Africa) Limited, and that “We are repeating the same case with Lotus Resources.”

a7075.speaker: Chifipa Mhango, Chief Economist, Don Consultancy Group (South Africa)
a7075.speech: Asked what advice law firm Omnia Strategy gave to Malawi's Attorney General: “One question that should be asked is what advice did law firm Omnia Strategy give to Malawi's Attorney General [Thabo Chakaka Nyirenda] when it offered for ‘free’ in the process towards the 2024 signing of the MDA? Did Omnia Strategy apply the advice or recommendations from ActionAid's June 2015 report to Malawi Government?”, while also revealing that Omnia Strategy was established by Cherie Blair, wife to former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, “who is a regular visitor to Malawi” ; “Omnia Strategy LLP company number in UK is OC368522, established by Cherie Blair, KC, which is a unique law firm that specialises on dispute resolution and prevention around the globe.”

a7075.speaker: Chifipa Mhango, Chief Economist, Don Consultancy Group (South Africa)
a7075.speech: Faulted the whole process of the new Kayelekera Mine deal with Lotus Resources, saying deal negotiations in any other industries “requires certain skills sets, and strong attributes in understanding the process and global industry at large” ; “Hence, there is a strong preference for CEOs in the sector that have strong business acumen and industry trends knowledge such as CAs, industrial economist, among others. Malawi has a vast mineral reserve, and if this trend of deal making continues in the sector, then we will continue to lose out. Uranium is in high demand in countries such as USA, France, and China — with a projected global demand indicating almost double by 2030, with a strong spot price. We need to wake up as the country and limit political involvement in mining deal making. The 85% and 15% arrangement does not reflect true asset value analysis, especially on what Malawi is getting from this lucrative mining operation, which is of lowest production cost globally. I am also concerned around the outcomes of the deal in relation to fiscal regime, in which there is zero export duties, as well as limited development obligations to Malawi in relation to the benefits accrued to Lotus Resources.”

a7075.speaker: Chifipa Mhango, Chief Economist, Don Consultancy Group (South Africa)
a7075.speech: Indicated that on Lotus Resources' offtake agreement with the North American utility company, signed on March 18, 2025, to sell 600,000lb of uranium from Kayelekera mine, if Malawi had signed a better deal it was bound to benefit massively as the deal is worth millions of US dollars: “According to World Nuclear Association report of May 2024, in Africa, we have Namibia, South Africa, Niger and Malawi with huge uranium reserves, featuring among the top 20 in the world. At times, our own actions and decisions impoverish us, as a country. It's high time we show our true patriotism towards our Malawi.”

a7075.speaker: Omnia Strategy (report of August 5, 2024)
a7075.speech: Described the MDA as “a significant milestone that promises to deliver welcome benefits to Malawi and its people while securing the future of a globally important mining asset in a peaceful democratic country” ; said Omnia Strategy and DWF were “privileged” to have worked closely with Malawi's Attorney General Chakaka Nyirenda “to support the Government and advise on the MDA with a view to upholding the country's interests and respecting Malawi's sovereignty and commitment to environmental, social and governance best international practice” ; “Working closely with DWF and consistent with a shared commitment to delivering elegant legal solutions in complex environments, Omnia and DWF's expert advice was delivered at zero cost to Malawi. At a time when State budgets are stretched, Omnia and DWF recognise the importance of finding innovative mechanisms to allow governments to prioritise health, education, security and others while not compromising the quality of the legal advice they need and deserve.”

a7075.speaker: ActionAid Malawi (report of June 2015)
a7075.speech: Described Malawi as the poorest country in the world, that lost out on US$43 million in revenue in six years up to 2015, “from a single company – the Australian mining company Paladin”: “The money has been lost through a combination of harmful tax incentives from the Malawian government, and tax planning using treaty shopping by Paladin”, adding that the US$43 million lost could have been used to pay for 8,500 annual salaries for medical doctors; 17,000 annual salaries for nurses; 39,000 annual teachers salaries; or 431,000 annual HIV/Aids treatments ; “What has happened is not illegal – on the contrary, the combination of tax breaks and tax planning that has resulted in this loss of crucial funds is a result of Malawian and international laws, treaties and agreements. People around the world are outraged that companies get away with paying less tax while the rest of us contribute our fair share. This report shows how governments and international tax rules allow this to happen.” ; “Tax matters; tax pays for public services such as education, health care and social services...
